turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Hale, quick one before the doctor calls you. The machine gave me 164 over 98, and your pulse was 76.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That isn't what I saw. I was looking over your shoulder, it said 152 over 90.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): I read 164 over 98, and that's what I've put down. I'm not going to average it with what you think you saw.

[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Honestly, the pair of you. I tense up the second that cuff goes on. Our one at home said one-thirty something this morning, which matches neither of you, so that's helpful. And can someone look at the radiator out there, it's like a fridge.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come on through, both of you. I'm Dr Shah. Grab a seat.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): This is Derek, my husband. He wouldn't let me come on my own. I said it's a cough, not a crisis, but he had the car keys already in his hand.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Start wherever you like. What's been bothering you?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): The cough, really. Dry little tickle, and then I'm off. I had a proper cold, and I reckon this is just the end of it hanging about. It's been weeks.
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been six weeks. It started before we went down to her sister's, I'm sure of that.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Six? No. Three weeks. The cold was the week they missed the bins, and the cough came on after that. I remember the bins.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're apart on it, so I won't force a single date. I'll note somewhere between three and six weeks, and leave the exact start open.

[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Good, because I couldn't tell you the day. It crept up. One minute I'm fine, next minute I'm coughing in the queue at the post office and the woman actually leans away from me.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does anything come up when you cough? Any phlegm?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing at all. Bone dry. It's worse when I'm talking, which is a shame, and it's worse in the cold air walking up from the bus.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, temperatures, sweats?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I was fluey and shivery when the cold had me, but that's finished. I finished the Lemsips and everything.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain in the chest, or a tight band when you cough?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No pain. Bit annoying, that's all.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. The hill by the chemist has always puffed me out, cough or no cough.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): And at night, does it wake you?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I'm up at five because the dog thinks dawn is a personal appointment. We got him from a rescue down in Truro, soft as anything, no sense of time.
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If she starts on the dog we'll be here till lunch. He's fine. She's the one coughing.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted, and the dog can stay out of the notes. You've had high blood pressure for a while, haven't you?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Years of it. I'm 64 and I feel completely well, which is why I forget to take it seriously. They keep changing the tablets on me.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me what you take these days, the names if you've got them, or just what you call them.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): There's the water tablet, every morning, donkey's years I've been on that. And the new one they gave me last time, ramipril.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): The record I have says ramipril 5 milligrams once a day, and it was started three weeks ago.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Five? The pharmacist told me ten, I'm almost sure. Little white ones. Mind you I had a lot of bags that day, I might have misheard.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I had a look in the cupboard. I thought the packet said 5 mg. I didn't bring it, though, so I wouldn't swear.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then the dose stays unconfirmed. I'm not choosing between 5 and 10 without the box.

[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): My brother in Leeds is on lisinopril, he was telling me. His blood pressure's been a proper nightmare and he still doesn't cough, he made sure I knew that. Then we got onto how awful the trains are, which took longer than the medical bit.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): His lisinopril isn't yours, so I'll leave it there. Do you use an inhaler, aspirin, anything for cholesterol?

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No inhaler. Atorvastatin at night, that's the cholesterol one, 20 milligrams. Aspirin I don't take. They mentioned it when I had a tooth out last year and I never started it.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the water tablet, do you actually know which one, or is it just the water tablet to you?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Just the water tablet. I nearly said indapamide then, but that's me guessing, I always get the name wrong. One each morning, makes me wee before I've had my tea.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fine, we won't invent a name. Have you been taking the ramipril every day as it was prescribed?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Most days. I missed a couple when we were at my daughter's with the grandchildren. So, not strictly.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose not. Nothing dramatic comes to mind. Penicillin was all right, that I do remember.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Never have. Horrible habit. Derek packed his in, but that's his story.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And a drink?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Glass of wine with Sunday lunch, if the roast hasn't gone wrong. Last Sunday the beef was a tragedy, so I didn't bother. Not a big drinker.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll have a listen if you lift your jumper a touch. Nice deep breaths. Your lungs are clear, no wheeze and no crackles. Heart sounds are normal.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh good. My neighbour had a shadow on a scan and it was just the way she was standing, whole week of fuss. I don't want one of those if I can help it.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): No scan today. I'm thinking it through rather than labelling it: this could be the tail of the cold, or it could be the ramipril, because that family of tablets makes some people cough. I can't rule either out, and it may be a bit of both, so I'm not going to call it one or the other.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): So you're not actually saying the tablet did it.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not. No firm diagnosis for the cough. What I am going to do is stop the ramipril you were started on for your blood pressure, and switch you to losartan 50 milligrams once a day.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Losartan. Right. There was a poster outside about faces swelling up. Is that this one?

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any of these blood pressure tablets can do that rarely. If your face, lips or tongue swell, or you get truly breathless, or chest pain, stop it and get help the same day. Keep taking the water tablet and the atorvastatin as usual.
[SEG0052] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And suppose the cough just sits there?
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it's still going when I see her next, we might arrange a chest x-ray. I'm not booking that now.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): When's next, then? Only the car's in for its MOT the Thursday after next, so not that morning, Derek will have a fit.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Four weeks from today, a planned check of the pressure and the cough. If things get worse before then, don't sit on it, come back or ring the surgery.
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): Four weeks. I'll try and keep the packet somewhere sensible. I once lost a library book for the best part of a year, so no promises.
[SEG0057] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll put the new ones by the kettle. She can't miss the kettle.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Once a day only, and if you miss a dose don't take two the next day. Whatever strength of ramipril is in the box, stop it, don't finish the strip just because it's there.
[SEG0059] person_1 (NURSE): I'll amend the list: ramipril stopped, dose left blank, losartan 50 milligrams to be started. I've kept both blood pressure readings rather than picking one.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Joan, anything you want to ask before you head off?
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): Will the cough actually go? And I'm only half joking about bringing the dog next time, he gets lonely. Well, I get lonely for him. You know.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't promise the cough will go, we haven't settled the cause. We'll look again in four weeks. The dog stays at home, I'm afraid.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): Worth a try. Come on, Derek, that parking meter won't extend itself. Thanks, doctor.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

omissions.text: Shortness of breath was specifically asked about and not clearly present: patient said 'Sometimes, not really' and that the hill by the chemist has always puffed her out, cough or no cough.
Night waking from cough was asked about and only equivocal: patient said 'Sometimes, not really.'
Aspirin is not taken; it was mentioned around a tooth extraction last year but she never started it.
No known medication allergies were identified when asked; patient said nothing dramatic comes to mind and recalled penicillin was all right.
